raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to provide transient vessel support and antiproliferative drug delivery, followed by scaffold resorption, with the hope of restoring vasomotion, permitting adaptive remodeling, simplifying future bypass grafting, and reducing very late events attributable to permanent metallic cages. Early first-in-human experience with the poly-L-lactide everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold was biologically compelling: feasibility was shown in 2007 [1], the ABSORB cohort A study demonstrated acceptable short-term safety [2], and serial angiography, intravascular ultrasound, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and vasomotor testing suggested progressive strut resorption and restoration of vasoreactivity [3]. Iteration to a second-generation scaffold improved radial integrity and imaging outcomes in ABSORB B [4,5].

The clinical turning point came when BVS were tested against contemporary cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (EES). ABSORB III met non-inferiority for 1-year target-lesion failure in selected, relatively non-complex lesions [6]. Similarly, ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan reported non-inferior early angiographic or clinical outcomes in regulated populations [7,8]. ABSORB II, however, failed to demonstrate the anticipated vasomotor advantage at 3 years and showed higher device-oriented events with BVS [9,10]. In the all-comers AIDA trial, BVS did not reduce target-vessel failure and was associated with substantially higher definite/probable device thrombosis than EES [11]. ABSORB IV, designed with improved implantation technique and exclusion of very small vessels, reduced early hazards but did not establish a clear clinical advantage [12].

Mechanistic explanations for these outcomes are now well defined. First-generation Absorb had thick struts, limited overexpansion tolerance, and susceptibility to underexpansion, malapposition, and late dismantling during polymer degradation. In ABSORB III, excess events through 3 years were especially related to target-vessel myocardial infarction and device thrombosis [13], whereas 5-year follow-up suggested that the period of excess risk diminished after complete resorption [14]. Imaging substudies reinforced the importance of scaffold expansion, embedded struts, avoidance of small vessels, and meticulous lesion preparation [15]. Pooled analyses confirmed that 1-year performance could appear acceptable in selected lesions [16], but 3-year patient-level data showed increased target-lesion failure and thrombosis with BVS [17]. Technique analyses led to the “PSP” approach—adequate predilatation, appropriate sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—as a practical framework for safer implantation [18].

Meta-analyses and network comparisons largely converged on the same conclusion: compared with second-generation EES, first-generation Absorb BVS increased myocardial infarction and scaffold thrombosis without a mortality benefit [19-23]. More recent pooled 5-year analyses refine rather than reverse that message: the hazard is front-loaded during the resorption phase, and outcomes after approximately 3 years may be similar to metallic EES, but the early penalty limits routine clinical utility [24,25].

Evidence in special populations has been mixed. In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, TROFI II showed comparable early healing by OCT in selected patients [26], but broader STEMI and registry experiences raised concern about thrombosis in thrombus-rich lesions and with suboptimal expansion. EVERBIO II and other smaller randomized studies suggested broadly similar angiographic late loss but were underpowered for clinical safety [27]. Registry and angiographic substudy data highlighted restenosis at scaffold margins, small-vessel risk, and learning-curve effects [28]. In propensity-matched STEMI comparisons, event rates were not reassuring enough to support unrestricted use [29]. COMPARE-ABSORB, focused on patients at high restenosis risk, again failed to show superiority of Absorb BVS over metallic drug-eluting stents [30].

Thus, first-generation BVS transformed thinking about “vascular restoration therapy” but not everyday PCI. Contemporary practice should not use first-generation Absorb BVS routinely outside research settings. The field’s future depends on thinner struts, faster and more predictable resorption, greater radial strength, improved deliverability, and imaging-guided implantation. Magnesium and next-generation polymeric or iron-based scaffolds may yet realize the concept, but they must demonstrate superiority or clear niche benefit against excellent modern drug-eluting stents with long-term, adequately powered randomized data.
